newsitem.title: INDIA: India's new PM wants Chidambaram's budget - speaker.
newsitem.headline: India's new PM wants Chidambaram's budget - speaker.

text.p: India's new prime minister, Inder Kumar Gujral, supports the pathbreaking budget proposed by former finance minister P. Chidambaram, the speaker of the lower house said on Monday.

P.A. Sangma told reporters after a meeting with Gujral that the prime minister wanted to push through the 1997/98 (April-March) budget that Chidambaram presented to parliament on February 28, sparking a rally in share prices.

But the house speaker said the budget plan, which has been held hostage by a three-week old political crisis that toppled former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, would not be taken up before April 30 to give Gujral time to settle into office.
"His (Gujral's) indication is he will go by the old budget," Sangma said, referring to Chidambaram's plan.
Gujral told reporters that he would pursue economic reforms but might make some minor changes in the budget.
"The economic policy on which our budget has been based will remain more or less the same, maybe some minor changes here or there," he said.

Chidambaram was not included in Gujral's cabinet as his regional Tamil Maanila Congress party decided on Saturday to stay out of the government because its leader, G.K. Moopanar, was not chosen to head Gujral's United Front coalition.

Chitta Basu of the All-India Forward Block party said parliament would adjourn on Tuesday after a vote of confidence in Gujral and reassemble on April 30 until May 16. Basu said the decision was taken by parliament's business advisory committee.
Gujral was expected to win the confidence vote as he was supported by his 15-party United Front coalition, with 178 votes in the 542-member lower house, and the Congress party, with 140.

Sangma said parliamentary officials were examining whether Gujral would have to re-introduce a budget or could simply leave the budget drafted by Chidambaram before parliament. "It is a procedural aspect which we have never faced earlier," he said.
The house speaker said the government hoped the lower house would approve the Finance Bill, which incorporates tax and tariff measures, by May 11 so that the president could sign it by May 14.
Human Resource Development Minister S.R. Bommai said Gujral, who kept the finance ministry portfolio for himself, might pilot a budget bill through parliament.
The budget, widely hailed by domestic industry and foreign investors, is considered a litmus test of the new government's resolve to press ahead with economic reforms.
